P(A, B, C) can be rewritten as P(C | A, B) * P(B | A) * P(A). This is because P(A, B, C) is the probability of A, B, and C occurring together, and we can think of it as the probability of C occurring given A and B, multiplied by the probability of B occurring given A, multiplied by the probability of A occurring.

Looking at the options, the one that matches this form is P(C | A, B) * P(B | A) * P(A).

The answer is (G).

question:
Let G = (V, E) be a finite directed acyclic graph with |E| > 0. Which of the following must be true?
I. G has a vertex with no incoming edge.
II. G has a vertex with no outgoing edge.
III. G has an isolated vertex, that is, one with neither an incoming edge nor an outgoing edge.

None of the above
I and II only
II and III only
I, II, and a vertex with one outgoing edge
I, II, and a vertex with one incoming edge
All of the above (I, II, III)
II only
I only
III only
model_outputs: In a directed acyclic graph (DAG), there must be at least one vertex with no incoming edges, as that would be the start of a path through the graph. Therefore, I must be true. However, there is no requirement that there must be a vertex with no outgoing edges, as every vertex could potentially have edges to other vertices, even in a DAG. This means II is not necessarily true. An isolated vertex, one with neither incoming nor outgoing edges, is not a requirement in a DAG, as vertices can be connected without having edges to vertices not already in the graph. Therefore, III is not necessarily true. The only statement that must be true is I, and the answer is (I).
